title: Meet the only known trebuchet casualty in history
excerpt: It highlights the brutality of medieval warfare," said paleopathologist Jo Buckberry.
content_html:
a large boulder the size of a small boulder

“It highlights the brutality of medieval warfare,” said paleopathologist Jo Buckberry.

This still from The Wolf at the Door, by Bob Marshall of Historic Environment Scotland, shows what the siege of Stirling Castle might have looked like, complete with trebuchets. Credit: Bob Marshall and HES

This still from The Wolf at the Door, by Bob Marshall of Historic Environment Scotland, shows what the siege of Stirling Castle might have looked like, complete with trebuchets. Credit: Bob Marshall and HES

During a medieval siege, a trebuchet scored a chance hit on an unlucky defender. A small boulder slammed into his upper back at close to 300 kilometers an hour, smashing bones and crushing him beneath its weight.

The man’s skeleton lay beneath the chapel of Scotland’s Stirling Castle, along with the remains of several other people who had clearly died violent deaths. But this one, known to us only as Skeleton 150 (or as “trebuchet guy” in your faithful correspondent’s notes), stood out even among that battle-damaged crowd because most of his upper body had been shattered. According to University of Bradford paleopathologist Jo Buckberry, who presented her research at the 25th European Meeting of the Paleopathology Association last week, Skeleton 150 is the only known trebuchet casualty in history.

A shattered skeleton

Skeleton 150 was in terrible shape, even for a dead guy. The man’s skull had broken in 61 separate places, and another 60 jagged bits of bone were distributed across his ribs. His right shoulder was broken, and his right leg above the knee was basically shattered.

Buckberry and her colleagues threw everything they could, metaphorically speaking, at the jigsaw puzzle of broken bones: forensics, microscopes, X-rays, and micro-CT scans. All of those results pointed to a single moment of crushing impact by something heavy and fast-moving. The pattern of the injuries suggests that the man’s right shoulder and the back of his head caught the brunt of the impact, while his ribs probably cracked under the weight of something heavy slamming him into the ground and pinning him there.

The bones had broken when they were fresh, so it was clearly not a case of “oops, we dropped a big rock on the corpse.” And the amount of force required to do so much damage in a single, shattering blow ruled out several messy possible ways to die during a medieval siege: Skeleton 150 hadn’t been trampled by a horse or run over by a cart, for example. Even if he had fallen from the castle walls, he probably wouldn’t have landed with enough force to do all of that, and the angle would have been all wrong.

“The most similar cases I was finding were car crashes and people hit by trains,” Buckberry told Science.org’s Andrew Curry. Assuming Stirling Castle hadn’t been attacked by time travelers, though, that raised new questions. “What is large and moving very quickly in 1304?”

Big rocks flung by trebuchets, that’s what.

The physics of throwing big rocks

A trebuchet works a bit like the world’s deadliest seesaw; at the long end of the seesaw is the sling that holds the projectile, and at the shorter end is a counterweight (a box of rocks or lead, 10 to 100 times heavier than the projectile). When the counterweight drops, its momentum raises the other end of the seesaw, tossing the sling up in a big arc. And when the sling reaches the end of its length, it stops—but the projectile keeps flying until it hits something.

A typical trebuchet of the time could launch a 90-kilogram projectile (typically a big rock) a few hundred yards. According to this handy medieval trebuchet calculator, that means the projectile would have smashed into Skeleton 150 at somewhere between 200 and 300 kilometers per hour, depending on the exact weight of the projectile and the trebuchet’s counterweight, the length of the sling, and the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow. That’s an impact with a little over 200 kilojoules of energy.

Trebuchets and other siege engines (we will, under no circumstances, be delving into the distinctions between the different types of catapults) were meant to take out walls and other fortifications. They weren’t anti-personnel weapons; people undoubtedly got injured by flying debris or collapsing structures, but medieval engineers weren’t aiming their catapults at individuals. Skeleton 150 just got terribly unlucky.

“While the use of siege engines is well-documented, we believe this is the first evidence of trebuchet trauma in the archaeological record,” wrote Buckberry, adding, “The lack of directly comparable forensic cases remains a limitation.”

Who was Skeleton 150? Scottish, probably

Skeleton 150 was one of nine people found in graves beneath the castle’s medieval chapel, to the surprise of renovation workers, in 1997. Five of the dead had wounds that suggested they had died violent deaths: a middle-aged woman had suffered two heavy blows to the side of her head before falling and being struck with a war-hammer, which left a pair of eerily-neat square holes in the top of her skull. A teenage boy had been stabbed in the chest with a sharp weapon that left its mark on his ribs, then struck hard in the jaw, collarbone, and torso.

It’s hard to say exactly who any of these people were, besides obvious medieval wartime casualties. All five of their remains were radiocarbon dated to around the Scottish Wars of Independence in the early 1300s, during which Stirling Castle was hotly contested real estate; it changed hands five times just in the eight years between 1296 and 1304, and the wars carried on until 1357. So some of the people buried in the chapel may have been Scottish, and others may have been English.

At least one of the dead, whose skeleton bore the marks of a lifetime of healed wounds, turned out to be an English knight, Sir John de Stricheley, who died in 1341. The ratio of chemical isotopes in his bones suggested that he had grown up eating food grown on the bedrock of southern England, and that, combined with his age and apparent status, pointed to an English knight. Sir John de Stricheley died at the castle in 1341 (and was important enough to have his death written down properly).

Buried not far from Sir John and the others lay Skeleton 150, who Buckberry and her colleagues say was most likely a Scottish defender of the castle killed during the siege of 1304, when King Edward I of England laid siege to Stirling Castle with what Historic Environment Scotland describes as “possibly the largest array of siege engines ever assembled by the kingdom of England.”

Setting the stage

In 1304, Skeleton 150 was probably one of the 25 men, led by Sir William Oliphant, who made up the last gasp of Scottish resistance against England and Edward I. After defeating William “They Will Never Take Our Freedom” Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk in 1298, Edward spent the next six years conquering the rest of Scotland. The country’s nobles eventually surrendered in exchange for being allowed to keep their lands (some of them may have done so with their fingers crossed). Edward’s long and bloody campaign was nearly over, except for this one castle, which inconveniently happened to perch along a strategically important road to Edinburgh. And the king was not amused.

In preparation for the siege, Edward decided to flex his newly won power over the Scots, which was undoubtedly as much a political gesture as a strategic choice. He ordered the Scottish nobles who had just surrendered to send him troops and horses for the siege, and he ordered that every church in Scotland strip the lead from their roofs and send it to the siege as well. Thirty-nine carts of lead arrived from around Scotland, mostly from St. Andrew’s, along with “all the iron and great stones of Glasgow.”

Thirteen siege engines were in place when Edward I arrived on the scene in April of 1304, and they bombarded the castle around the clock for three solid months. Somewhere during those months, Skeleton 150 met a bad end.

The War Wolf

As the siege wore on, Edward I set his engineers and carpenters to work on the largest trebuchet anyone in the world had ever seen. He dubbed it the War Wolf, or Loup de Guerre, and it was an absolute monster—so much so that Oliphant, who had held the castle for three months and still had enough men and provisions to keep antagonizing the king for a while yet, decided that actually, he would very much like to surrender after all, before the giant trebuchet took the field, thank you very much.

And Edward I told him no.

The king was not going to miss the chance to use his tremendous new trebuchet, nor the chance to very publicly and definitively (and also literally) crush the last of the Scottish opposition to his reign. So he ordered his engineers to load the War Wolf and fling a 140-kilogram projectile straight through the castle’s curtain wall. Witnesses compared it to watching an arrow pierce a paper target.

It’s tempting to speculate that Skeleton 150 might have been a casualty of the infamous War Wolf itself, but that seems unlikely. For one thing, the odds just aren’t in favor of the theory; the War Wolf flung a single, albeit enormous, shot on the very last day of the siege. Thirteen other siege engines had been firing at all hours of the day and night for three months before that.

He was probably dead and hastily buried in the chapel by the time the castle walls crumbled and Oliphant and the other survivors were rounded up and taken south to prison in England.

Kiona is a freelance science journalist and resident archaeology nerd at Ars Technica.

blocks.html_en: A typical trebuchet of the time could launch a 90-kilogram projectile (typically a big rock) a few hundred yards. According to this handy medieval trebuchet calculator, that means the projectile would have smashed into Skeleton 150 at somewhere between 200 and 300 kilometers per hour, depending on the exact weight of the projectile and the trebuchet’s counterweight, the length of the sling, and the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow. That’s an impact with a little over 200 kilojoules of energy.

sentences.en: A typical trebuchet of the time could launch a 90-kilogram projectile (typically a big rock) a few hundred yards.
sentences.zh: 当时的典型投石机可以将 90 公斤重的射弹（通常是一块大石头）发射到几百码外。

sentences.en: According to this handy medieval trebuchet calculator, that means the projectile would have smashed into Skeleton 150 at somewhere between 200 and 300 kilometers per hour, depending on the exact weight of the projectile and the trebuchet’s counterweight, the length of the sling, and the airspeed velocity of an unladen swallow.
sentences.zh: 根据这个方便的中世纪投石机计算器，这意味着抛射物将以每小时 200 到 300 公里之间的速度撞向 Skeleton 150，具体取决于抛射物的确切重量和投石机的配重、吊索的长度以及空载燕子的空速。

sentences.en: That’s an impact with a little over 200 kilojoules of energy.
sentences.zh: 这是一个略高于 200 千焦的能量的冲击。

blocks.html_en: Trebuchets and other siege engines (we will, under no circumstances, be delving into the distinctions between the different types of catapults) were meant to take out walls and other fortifications. They weren’t anti-personnel weapons; people undoubtedly got injured by flying debris or collapsing structures, but medieval engineers weren’t aiming their catapults at individuals. Skeleton 150 just got terribly unlucky.

blocks.html_en: “While the use of siege engines is well-documented, we believe this is the first evidence of trebuchet trauma in the archaeological record,” wrote Buckberry, adding, “The lack of directly comparable forensic cases remains a limitation.”

blocks.html_en: Who was Skeleton 150? Scottish, probably

sentences.en: Who was Skeleton 150?
sentences.zh: 骷髅150是谁？

sentences.en: Scottish, probably
sentences.zh: 苏格兰人，可能

blocks.html_en: Skeleton 150 was one of nine people found in graves beneath the castle’s medieval chapel, to the surprise of renovation workers, in 1997. Five of the dead had wounds that suggested they had died violent deaths: a middle-aged woman had suffered two heavy blows to the side of her head before falling and being struck with a war-hammer, which left a pair of eerily-neat square holes in the top of her skull. A teenage boy had been stabbed in the chest with a sharp weapon that left its mark on his ribs, then struck hard in the jaw, collarbone, and torso.

sentences.en: Skeleton 150 was one of nine people found in graves beneath the castle’s medieval chapel, to the surprise of renovation workers, in 1997.
sentences.zh: 1997 年，令整修工人惊讶的是，150 号骷髅是在城堡中世纪教堂下方的坟墓中发现的九具尸体之一。

sentences.en: Five of the dead had wounds that suggested they had died violent deaths: a middle-aged woman had suffered two heavy blows to the side of her head before falling and being struck with a war-hammer, which left a pair of eerily-neat square holes in the top of her skull.
sentences.zh: 其中五名死者身上的伤口表明他们是死于暴力：一名中年妇女的头部侧面遭受了两次重击，然后摔倒并被战锤击中，在她的头骨顶部留下了两个奇怪的整齐的方形孔。

sentences.en: A teenage boy had been stabbed in the chest with a sharp weapon that left its mark on his ribs, then struck hard in the jaw, collarbone, and torso.
sentences.zh: 一名十几岁男孩的胸部被锋利的武器刺伤，在他的肋骨上留下了痕迹，然后下巴、锁骨和躯干被重击。

blocks.html_en: It’s hard to say exactly who any of these people were, besides obvious medieval wartime casualties. All five of their remains were radiocarbon dated to around the Scottish Wars of Independence in the early 1300s, during which Stirling Castle was hotly contested real estate; it changed hands five times just in the eight years between 1296 and 1304, and the wars carried on until 1357. So some of the people buried in the chapel may have been Scottish, and others may have been English.

sentences.en: It’s hard to say exactly who any of these people were, besides obvious medieval wartime casualties.
sentences.zh: 除了明显的中世纪战时伤亡之外，很难确切地说出这些人是谁。

sentences.en: All five of their remains were radiocarbon dated to around the Scottish Wars of Independence in the early 1300s, during which Stirling Castle was hotly contested real estate; it changed hands five times just in the eight years between 1296 and 1304, and the wars carried on until 1357.
sentences.zh: 他们的五具遗骸均经放射性碳测年，年代可追溯至 1300 年代初苏格兰独立战争期间，在此期间，斯特灵城堡是备受争议的房地产地盘。仅在1296年至1304年的八年间，它就易手五次，战争一直持续到1357年。

sentences.en: So some of the people buried in the chapel may have been Scottish, and others may have been English.
sentences.zh: 因此，埋葬在教堂里的一些人可能是苏格兰人，其他人可能是英国人。

blocks.html_en: At least one of the dead, whose skeleton bore the marks of a lifetime of healed wounds, turned out to be an English knight, Sir John de Stricheley, who died in 1341. The ratio of chemical isotopes in his bones suggested that he had grown up eating food grown on the bedrock of southern England, and that, combined with his age and apparent status, pointed to an English knight. Sir John de Stricheley died at the castle in 1341 (and was important enough to have his death written down properly).

sentences.en: At least one of the dead, whose skeleton bore the marks of a lifetime of healed wounds, turned out to be an English knight, Sir John de Stricheley, who died in 1341.
sentences.zh: 至少其中一名死者的骨架上有一生愈合伤口的痕迹，结果证明他是一位英国骑士约翰·德·斯特里切利爵士 (Sir John de Stricheley)，于 1341 年去世。

sentences.en: The ratio of chemical isotopes in his bones suggested that he had grown up eating food grown on the bedrock of southern England, and that, combined with his age and apparent status, pointed to an English knight.
sentences.zh: 他骨骼中化学同位素的比例表明他是吃英格兰南部基岩上种植的食物长大的，结合他的年龄和明显的地位，表明他是一位英国骑士。

sentences.en: Sir John de Stricheley died at the castle in 1341 (and was important enough to have his death written down properly).
sentences.zh: 1341 年，约翰·德·斯特里奇利爵士 (Sir John de Stracheley) 在城堡去世（他的死因非常重要，因此被正确地记录下来）。

blocks.html_en: Buried not far from Sir John and the others lay Skeleton 150, who Buckberry and her colleagues say was most likely a Scottish defender of the castle killed during the siege of 1304, when King Edward I of England laid siege to Stirling Castle with what Historic Environment Scotland describes as “possibly the largest array of siege engines ever assembled by the kingdom of England.”

sentences.en: Buried not far from Sir John and the others lay Skeleton 150, who Buckberry and her colleagues say was most likely a Scottish defender of the castle killed during the siege of 1304, when King Edward I of England laid siege to Stirling Castle with what Historic Environment Scotland describes as “possibly the largest array of siege engines ever assembled by the kingdom of England.”
sentences.zh: 埋葬在距离约翰爵士和其他人不远的地方的是 150 号骷髅，巴克伯里和她的同事说，她很可能是在 1304 年围攻期间被杀的苏格兰城堡守卫者，当时英格兰国王爱德华一世围攻斯特灵城堡，苏格兰历史环境组织将其描述为“可能是英格兰王国有史以来组装的最大的攻城器械阵列”。

blocks.html_en: Setting the stage

sentences.en: Setting the stage
sentences.zh: 搭建舞台

blocks.html_en: In 1304, Skeleton 150 was probably one of the 25 men, led by Sir William Oliphant, who made up the last gasp of Scottish resistance against England and Edward I. After defeating William “They Will Never Take Our Freedom” Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk in 1298, Edward spent the next six years conquering the rest of Scotland. The country’s nobles eventually surrendered in exchange for being allowed to keep their lands (some of them may have done so with their fingers crossed). Edward’s long and bloody campaign was nearly over, except for this one castle, which inconveniently happened to perch along a strategically important road to Edinburgh. And the king was not amused.

sentences.en: In 1304, Skeleton 150 was probably one of the 25 men, led by Sir William Oliphant, who made up the last gasp of Scottish resistance against England and Edward I.
sentences.zh: 1304 年，骷髅 150 可能是威廉·奥利芬特爵士 (Sir William Oliphant) 率领的 25 人之一，他在苏格兰抵抗英格兰和爱德华一世的最后一搏中做出了最后的努力。

sentences.en: After defeating William “They Will Never Take Our Freedom” Wallace at the Battle of Falkirk in 1298, Edward spent the next six years conquering the rest of Scotland.
sentences.zh: 1298 年，爱德华在福尔柯克战役中击败“他们永远不会夺走我们的自由”的威廉·华莱士后，在接下来的六年里征服了苏格兰其他地区。

sentences.en: The country’s nobles eventually surrendered in exchange for being allowed to keep their lands (some of them may have done so with their fingers crossed).
sentences.zh: 该国的贵族最终投降，以换取保留自己土地的权利（其中一些人可能已经祈祷）。

sentences.en: Edward’s long and bloody campaign was nearly over, except for this one castle, which inconveniently happened to perch along a strategically important road to Edinburgh.
sentences.zh: 爱德华漫长而血腥的战役即将结束，除了这座城堡，它碰巧坐落在通往爱丁堡的一条具有重要战略意义的道路上。

sentences.en: And the king was not amused.
sentences.zh: 国王并不觉得好笑。

blocks.html_en: In preparation for the siege, Edward decided to flex his newly won power over the Scots, which was undoubtedly as much a political gesture as a strategic choice. He ordered the Scottish nobles who had just surrendered to send him troops and horses for the siege, and he ordered that every church in Scotland strip the lead from their roofs and send it to the siege as well. Thirty-nine carts of lead arrived from around Scotland, mostly from St. Andrew’s, along with “all the iron and great stones of Glasgow.”

sentences.en: In preparation for the siege, Edward decided to flex his newly won power over the Scots, which was undoubtedly as much a political gesture as a strategic choice.
sentences.zh: 在准备围攻时，爱德华决定向苏格兰人展示他新赢得的权力，这无疑既是一种政治姿态，也是一种战略选择。

sentences.en: He ordered the Scottish nobles who had just surrendered to send him troops and horses for the siege, and he ordered that every church in Scotland strip the lead from their roofs and send it to the siege as well.
sentences.zh: 他命令刚刚投降的苏格兰贵族派兵马去围攻，还命令苏格兰的每座教堂都把屋顶上的铅剥下来，也送去围攻。

sentences.en: Thirty-nine carts of lead arrived from around Scotland, mostly from St. Andrew’s, along with “all the iron and great stones of Glasgow.”
sentences.zh: 三十九辆铅车从苏格兰各地运来，其中大部分是从圣安德鲁斯运来的，还有“格拉斯哥所有的铁和大石头”。

blocks.html_en: Thirteen siege engines were in place when Edward I arrived on the scene in April of 1304, and they bombarded the castle around the clock for three solid months. Somewhere during those months, Skeleton 150 met a bad end.

sentences.en: Thirteen siege engines were in place when Edward I arrived on the scene in April of 1304, and they bombarded the castle around the clock for three solid months.
sentences.zh: 1304 年 4 月，当爱德华一世抵达现场时，十三辆攻城器械已就位，它们对城堡进行了长达三个月的全天候轰炸。

sentences.en: Somewhere during those months, Skeleton 150 met a bad end.
sentences.zh: 在那几个月的某个时候，Skeleton 150 遭遇了糟糕的结局。

blocks.html_en: The War Wolf

sentences.en: The War Wolf
sentences.zh: 战狼

blocks.html_en: As the siege wore on, Edward I set his engineers and carpenters to work on the largest trebuchet anyone in the world had ever seen. He dubbed it the War Wolf, or Loup de Guerre, and it was an absolute monster—so much so that Oliphant, who had held the castle for three months and still had enough men and provisions to keep antagonizing the king for a while yet, decided that actually, he would very much like to surrender after all, before the giant trebuchet took the field, thank you very much.

sentences.en: As the siege wore on, Edward I set his engineers and carpenters to work on the largest trebuchet anyone in the world had ever seen.
sentences.zh: 随着围困的持续，爱德华一世让他的工程师和木匠开始建造世界上最大的投石机。

sentences.en: He dubbed it the War Wolf, or Loup de Guerre, and it was an absolute monster—so much so that Oliphant, who had held the castle for three months and still had enough men and provisions to keep antagonizing the king for a while yet, decided that actually, he would very much like to surrender after all, before the giant trebuchet took the field, thank you very much.
sentences.zh: 他称它为“战狼”，或者“Loup de Guerre”，它是一个绝对的怪物——以至于奥利芬特已经占领了城堡三个月，仍然有足够的人员和物资继续与国王对抗一段时间，他决定，实际上，他很想在巨型投石机上场之前投降，非常感谢。

blocks.html_en: And Edward I told him no.

sentences.en: And Edward I told him no.
sentences.zh: 爱德华我告诉他不。

blocks.html_en: The king was not going to miss the chance to use his tremendous new trebuchet, nor the chance to very publicly and definitively (and also literally) crush the last of the Scottish opposition to his reign. So he ordered his engineers to load the War Wolf and fling a 140-kilogram projectile straight through the castle’s curtain wall. Witnesses compared it to watching an arrow pierce a paper target.

sentences.en: The king was not going to miss the chance to use his tremendous new trebuchet, nor the chance to very publicly and definitively (and also literally) crush the last of the Scottish opposition to his reign.
sentences.zh: 国王不会错过使用他巨大的新型投石机的机会，也不会错过公开、明确（而且字面上）粉碎苏格兰最后反对他统治的机会的机会。

sentences.en: So he ordered his engineers to load the War Wolf and fling a 140-kilogram projectile straight through the castle’s curtain wall.
sentences.zh: 于是，他命令工程师给战狼装弹，将一枚 140 公斤重的炮弹直接射穿城堡的幕墙。

sentences.en: Witnesses compared it to watching an arrow pierce a paper target.
sentences.zh: 目击者将其比作观看箭射穿纸靶。

blocks.html_en: It’s tempting to speculate that Skeleton 150 might have been a casualty of the infamous War Wolf itself, but that seems unlikely. For one thing, the odds just aren’t in favor of the theory; the War Wolf flung a single, albeit enormous, shot on the very last day of the siege. Thirteen other siege engines had been firing at all hours of the day and night for three months before that.

sentences.zh: 人们很容易猜测 Skeleton 150 可能是臭名昭著的战狼本身的受害者，但这似乎不太可能。

sentences.zh: 在此之前的三个月里，另外十三辆攻城车已经日夜不停地开火。

blocks.html_en: He was probably dead and hastily buried in the chapel by the time the castle walls crumbled and Oliphant and the other survivors were rounded up and taken south to prison in England.

content_html_zh:
一块小石头大小的大石头

“它突显了中世纪战争的残酷性，”古病理学家乔·巴克伯里说。

这张剧照来自苏格兰历史环境局的鲍勃·马歇尔拍摄的《门口的狼》，展示了斯特灵城堡的围攻可能是什么样子，并配备了投石机。 图片来源：Bob Marshall 和 HES

这张剧照来自苏格兰历史环境局的鲍勃·马歇尔拍摄的《门口的狼》，展示了斯特灵城堡的围攻可能是什么样子，并配备了投石机。 图片来源：Bob Marshall 和 HES

在中世纪的一次围攻中，投石机偶然击中了一名不幸的防守者。 一块小石块以接近每小时 300 公里的速度撞到了他的上背部，粉碎了他的骨头，把他压垮了。

这名男子的骨架躺在苏格兰斯特灵城堡的教堂下方，旁边还有其他几人的遗骸，这些人显然是死于暴力。 但这个被我们只知道为“骷髅 150”（或者在忠实记者的笔记中称为“投石手”）的人，甚至在那些饱受战争摧残的人群中也很引人注目，因为他的上半身大部分都被打碎了。 布拉德福德大学古病理学家 Jo Buckberry 上周在古病理学协会第 25 届欧洲会议上展示了她的研究成果，据她介绍，Skeleton 150 是历史上唯一已知的投石机伤亡事件。

破碎的骷髅

骷髅 150 的状况很糟糕，即使对于一个死人来说也是如此。 这名男子的头骨有 61 个不同的地方骨折，另外 60 块锯齿状的骨头分布在他的肋骨上。 右肩骨折，右腿膝盖以上基本粉碎。

打个比方来说，巴克贝里和她的同事们在骨折拼图上投入了一切：法医、显微镜、X 射线和微型 CT 扫描。 所有这些结果都表明，在某个瞬间，有重物和快速移动的物体造成了毁灭性的撞击。 受伤的情况表明，该男子的右肩和后脑勺首当其冲，而他的肋骨可能在重物的重压下破裂，将他撞到地上并将他固定在那里。

骨头在新鲜的时候就已经折断了，所以这显然不是“哎呀，我们在尸体上扔了一块大石头”的情况。 而且，在中世纪围攻期间，一次粉碎性打击造成如此大的伤害所需的力量排除了几种可能的死法：例如，Skeleton 150 没有被马践踏或被马车碾过。 即使他从城墙上掉下来，他也可能没有足够的力量来完成这一切，而且角度也会完全错误。

“我发现的最相似的案例是车祸和火车撞人，”巴克伯里告诉 Science.org 的安德鲁·库里。 不过，假设斯特灵城堡没有受到时间旅行者的袭击，这就引发了新的问题。 “1304年有什么东西很大而且移动得很快？”

投石机投掷大石头，就是这样。

扔大石头的物理原理

投石机的工作原理有点像世界上最致命的跷跷板。跷跷板的长端是固定弹丸的吊索，短端是配重（一盒岩石或铅，比弹丸重 10 到 100 倍）。 当配重下降时，其动量会抬起跷跷板的另一端，将吊索抛起一个大弧线。 当吊带到达其长度末端时，它会停止，但射弹会继续飞行，直到撞到某物。

当时的典型投石机可以将 90 公斤重的射弹（通常是一块大石头）发射到几百码外。 根据这个方便的中世纪投石机计算器，这意味着抛射物将以每小时 200 到 300 公里之间的速度撞向 Skeleton 150，具体取决于抛射物的确切重量和投石机的配重、吊索的长度以及空载燕子的空速。 这是一个略高于 200 千焦的能量的冲击。

投石机和其他攻城器械（在任何情况下，我们都不会深入研究不同类型的弹射器之间的区别）是为了摧毁城墙和其他防御工事。 它们不是杀伤人员武器；而是杀伤性武器。毫无疑问，人们会因飞溅的碎片或倒塌的建筑物而受伤，但中世纪的工程师并没有将弹射器瞄准个人。 骷髅150实​​在是太不走运了。

巴克伯里写道：“虽然攻城器械的使用有据可查，但我们相信这是考古记录中第一个关于投石机创伤的证据。”他补充道，“缺乏直接可比的法医案例仍然是一个限制。”

骷髅150是谁？ 苏格兰人，可能

1997 年，令整修工人惊讶的是，150 号骷髅是在城堡中世纪教堂下方的坟墓中发现的九具尸体之一。 其中五名死者身上的伤口表明他们是死于暴力：一名中年妇女的头部侧面遭受了两次重击，然后摔倒并被战锤击中，在她的头骨顶部留下了两个奇怪的整齐的方形孔。 一名十几岁男孩的胸部被锋利的武器刺伤，在他的肋骨上留下了痕迹，然后下巴、锁骨和躯干被重击。

除了明显的中世纪战时伤亡之外，很难确切地说出这些人是谁。 他们的五具遗骸均经放射性碳测年，年代可追溯至 1300 年代初苏格兰独立战争期间，在此期间，斯特灵城堡是备受争议的房地产地盘。仅在1296年至1304年的八年间，它就易手五次，战争一直持续到1357年。 因此，埋葬在教堂里的一些人可能是苏格兰人，其他人可能是英国人。

至少其中一名死者的骨架上有一生愈合伤口的痕迹，结果证明他是一位英国骑士约翰·德·斯特里切利爵士 (Sir John de Stricheley)，于 1341 年去世。 他骨骼中化学同位素的比例表明他是吃英格兰南部基岩上种植的食物长大的，结合他的年龄和明显的地位，表明他是一位英国骑士。 1341 年，约翰·德·斯特里奇利爵士 (Sir John de Stracheley) 在城堡去世（他的死因非常重要，因此被正确地记录下来）。

埋葬在距离约翰爵士和其他人不远的地方的是 150 号骷髅，巴克伯里和她的同事说，她很可能是在 1304 年围攻期间被杀的苏格兰城堡守卫者，当时英格兰国王爱德华一世围攻斯特灵城堡，苏格兰历史环境组织将其描述为“可能是英格兰王国有史以来组装的最大的攻城器械阵列”。

搭建舞台

1304 年，骷髅 150 可能是威廉·奥利芬特爵士 (Sir William Oliphant) 率领的 25 人之一，他在苏格兰抵抗英格兰和爱德华一世的最后一搏中做出了最后的努力。 1298 年，爱德华在福尔柯克战役中击败“他们永远不会夺走我们的自由”的威廉·华莱士后，在接下来的六年里征服了苏格兰其他地区。 该国的贵族最终投降，以换取保留自己土地的权利（其中一些人可能已经祈祷）。 爱德华漫长而血腥的战役即将结束，除了这座城堡，它碰巧坐落在通往爱丁堡的一条具有重要战略意义的道路上。 国王并不觉得好笑。

在准备围攻时，爱德华决定向苏格兰人展示他新赢得的权力，这无疑既是一种政治姿态，也是一种战略选择。 他命令刚刚投降的苏格兰贵族派兵马去围攻，还命令苏格兰的每座教堂都把屋顶上的铅剥下来，也送去围攻。 三十九辆铅车从苏格兰各地运来，其中大部分是从圣安德鲁斯运来的，还有“格拉斯哥所有的铁和大石头”。

1304 年 4 月，当爱德华一世抵达现场时，十三辆攻城器械已就位，它们对城堡进行了长达三个月的全天候轰炸。 在那几个月的某个时候，Skeleton 150 遭遇了糟糕的结局。

战狼

随着围困的持续，爱德华一世让他的工程师和木匠开始建造世界上最大的投石机。 他称它为“战狼”，或者“Loup de Guerre”，它是一个绝对的怪物——以至于奥利芬特已经占领了城堡三个月，仍然有足够的人员和物资继续与国王对抗一段时间，他决定，实际上，他很想在巨型投石机上场之前投降，非常感谢。

爱德华我告诉他不。

国王不会错过使用他巨大的新型投石机的机会，也不会错过公开、明确（而且字面上）粉碎苏格兰最后反对他统治的机会的机会。 于是，他命令工程师给战狼装弹，将一枚 140 公斤重的炮弹直接射穿城堡的幕墙。 目击者将其比作观看箭射穿纸靶。

人们很容易猜测 Skeleton 150 可能是臭名昭著的战狼本身的受害者，但这似乎不太可能。 一方面，这一理论的可能性并不大；战狼在围攻的最后一天发射了一发子弹，虽然数量巨大。 在此之前的三个月里，另外十三辆攻城车已经日夜不停地开火。

当城堡的城墙倒塌，奥利芬特和其他幸存者被围捕并送往南方英格兰的监狱时，他可能已经死了，并被匆忙埋在教堂里。

Kiona 是一名自由科学记者，也是 Ars Technica 的常驻考古学呆子。
